title: A practical week of Stoic thinking
summary: For anyone curious about Stoicism: six daily steps from checking your first impressions to a fair evening review, each building on the one before.

steps.title: Pause before you believe your first impression of an event
steps.body: Epictetus taught that people are upset less by events than by the judgments they attach to them. Your first impression arrives fast: "she ignored me" or "this is a disaster". Treat it as a claim you can test, not as a fact, and ask what you actually saw or heard.
steps.deeper:
The Stoics separated the raw event from the story the mind adds on top. Once you see the two as separate, you gain a short gap in which to choose your reaction. Founders of modern cognitive therapy credited Stoic writers as an influence, because the method is the same: check the thought before you act on the feeling.

A friend does not reply to your message all day. The first impression says they are annoyed with you. What you actually know is only that there was no reply. They could be busy, out of battery, or waiting until they can write properly. The event is the silence, and the annoyance is the part you added.

Catch one strong reaction today and write two lines about it: what I saw or heard, and what I added. Cross out the second line if you cannot check it, and act only on the first.

steps.title: Expect difficult people before you meet them
steps.body: Marcus Aurelius began his private notes with a morning rehearsal: today he would meet meddling, ungrateful and arrogant people. He reminded himself they act from a mistaken sense of what is good. Expecting them takes away the shock that feeds anger.
steps.deeper:
Surprise adds a layer to every annoyance. When you are caught off guard, you react first and think later. Rehearsing the encounter in advance removes the surprise. Marcus also gave himself a reason for patience: people who behave badly are usually working from mistaken ideas about what is good, and that is easier to meet with firmness than with hatred.

There is a colleague who interrupts in every Monday meeting. Instead of waiting to be irritated, you decide beforehand that the first interruption will pass without comment, and that you will finish your sentence at the same calm pace. When it happens, you are following a plan rather than being ambushed.

Name one person you will probably find difficult today. Write one sentence about what they are likely to do, and one calm sentence you will say or one thing you will let go.

steps.title: An insult only stings if you agree to it
steps.body: Epictetus argued that the person who insults you does not harm you. What harms you is your judgment that you have been harmed. So when a remark lands, sort it: if it is true, it is useful feedback, and if it is false, it describes the speaker, not you.
steps.deeper:
An insult has two parts: the words, and the meaning you give them. The Stoics held that only the second part is up to you. Asking whether the remark is true turns a sting into a decision. Either you learn something, or you let a false claim fall away without having to win an argument.

A coworker jokes that you are always late. If you were late twice this week, the remark is accurate, and you can fix it without feeling attacked. If you were not, it tells you about their mood or their habit of teasing. In both cases you stay in charge of what happens next.

Ask two questions the next time a comment stings: is any of it true, and is it worth a reply? Give yourself ten minutes before you answer, and write down what you decide.

steps.title: Add the words "if nothing prevents it" to your plans
steps.body: Seneca described a wise person who holds every plan with a quiet reserve: I will sail, unless something prevents it. You still give full effort. But if the plan fails, you are not shocked, because you had already allowed that it might.
steps.deeper:
Frustration is largely the gap between what you expected and what happened. A plan held with a reserve narrows that gap, because the possibility of interruption was part of the plan from the start. Seneca's point is about the mind, not about backup schedules: you commit to the effort and keep the outcome loosely held.

You plan a run at 8 on Saturday. You think to yourself, I will run at 8 if nothing prevents it. Rain arrives. Instead of feeling robbed, you notice that this is what the reserve was for, and you do a short indoor session or move the run to the afternoon.

Pick one plan that matters today and say it with the reserve attached: I will do this, if nothing prevents it. Then give it full effort, and if you are blocked, say out loud that the reserve has been used.

steps.title: Borrow the eyes of someone you admire in a hard moment
steps.body: Seneca advised choosing a person of good character and living as if they were watching. The aim is not fear of being judged but steadiness. In one of his letters he suggests picking a figure like Cato and measuring your conduct against that person.
steps.deeper:
It is hard to apply a vague rule such as be better. It is easier to picture a specific person and ask what they would do next. The imagined witness makes your standard concrete and gives you a pause between the impulse and the action. It also helps that the person is not you, so you are less likely to excuse yourself.

You are about to answer a rude email with an equally rude one. You picture a mentor you respect reading over your shoulder. You notice they would take a breath, state the facts, and ask one clear question. You write that email instead.

Choose one person, real or historical, whose conduct you respect. Write their name at the top of tomorrow's to-do list, and at the first tense moment ask yourself what they would do in your place.

steps.title: Close the day by reviewing it as a fair judge, not a prosecutor
steps.body: Seneca describes the philosopher Sextius asking himself each night what fault he had resisted and how he had improved. Seneca did the same once the lamp was out. The point is honest review without cruelty: face what happened, forgive it, and plan the fix.
steps.deeper:
A review turns a day of events into a lesson. Doing it at night, while the details are fresh, lets you correct small errors before they become habits. The tone matters: harsh self-attack makes people avoid the review, while a fair and forgiving tone keeps them coming back. That steady return is what builds character over weeks.

Tonight you replay the day. You snapped at a flatmate over dishes, which you regret. You also listened well in a meeting, which you are glad of. The fix is small and specific: tomorrow you will take one breath before answering when you feel irritated.

Write three short answers before sleep: what did I handle well, where did I fall short, and what will I do differently tomorrow. Stop after five minutes, and repeat it each night this week.
